entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.25.1">Lev 25:1</reference> <div eID="gen1495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1496" type="x-p"/> The law for the sabbatical and jubilee years brings to a close the laws given to Moses by Jehovah upon Mount Sinai. This is shown by the words of the heading (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.1">Lev 25:1</reference>), which point back to <reference osisRef="Exod.34.32">Exo 34:32</reference>, and bind together into an inward unity the whole round of laws that Moses received from God upon the mountain, and then gradually announced to the people. The same words are repeated, not only in <reference osisRef="Lev.7.38">Lev 7:38</reference> at the close of the laws of sacrifice, but also at <reference osisRef="Lev.26.46">Lev 26:46</reference>, at the close of the promises and threats which follow the law for the sabbatical and jubilee years, and lastly, at <reference osisRef="Lev.27.34">Lev 27:34</reference>, after the supplementary law concerning vows. The institution of the jubilee years corresponds to the institution of the day of atonement (ch. 16). Just as all the sins and uncleannesses of the whole congregation, which had remained unatoned for and uncleansed in the course of the year, were to be wiped away by the all-embracing expiation of the yearly recurring day of atonement, and an undisturbed relation to be restored between Jehovah and His people; so, by the appointment of the year of jubilee, the disturbance and confusion of the divinely appointed relations, which had been introduced in the course of time through the inconstancy of all human or earthly things, were to be removed by the appointment of the year of jubilee, and the kingdom of Israel to be brought back to its original condition. The next chapter (ch. 26) bears the same relation to the giving of the law upon Sinai as <reference osisRef="Exod.23.20-Exod.23.33">Exo 23:20-33</reference> to the covenant rights in <reference osisRef="Exod.20.22-Exod.20.23">Ex 20:22-23</reference>:19.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.25.2-Lev.25.4">Lev 25:2-4</reference> <div eID="gen1496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1497" type="x-p"/> The Sabbatical Year. - When Israel had come into the land which the Lord gave to it, it was to sanctify it to the Lord by the observance of a Sabbath. As the nation at large, with its labourers and beasts of burden, was to keep a Sabbath or day of rest every seventh day of the week, so the land which they filled was to rest (to keep, שׁבּי שׁבת as in <reference osisRef="Lev.23.32">Lev 23:32</reference>) a Sabbath to the Lord. Six years they were to sow the field and cut the vineyard, i.e., cultivate the corn-fields, vineyards, and olive-yards (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.11">Exo 23:11</reference> : see the remarks on <hi type="italic">cerem</hi> at <reference osisRef="Lev.19.10">Lev 19:10</reference>), and gather in their produce; but in the seventh year the land was to keep a Sabbath of rest (<hi type="italic">Sabbath</hi> <hi type="italic">sabbathon</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.31.15">Exo 31:15</reference>), a Sabbath consecrated to the Lord (see <reference osisRef="Exod.20.10">Exo 20:10</reference>); and in this year the land was neither to be tilled nor reaped (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.23.10-Exod.23.11">Exo 23:10-11</reference>). זמר in <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> applies only to the cutting of grapes, and so also in <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.6">Isa 5:6</reference>; hence <hi type="italic">zemorah</hi>, a vine-branch (Num 13:23), and <hi type="italic">mazmerah</hi>, a pruning-knife (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Isa 2:4</reference>, etc.).<note placement="foot">The meaning to sin and play, which is peculiar to the Piel, and is derived from <hi type="italic">zamar</hi>, to hum, has hardly anything to do with this. At all events the connection has not yet been shown to be a probable one. See <hi type="italic">Hupfeld</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1-Ps.4.8">Psa 4:1-8</reference> pp. 421-2, note.</note> <div eID="gen1497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1498" type="x-p"/> The omission of sowing and reaping presupposed that the sabbatical year commenced with the civil year, in the autumn of the sixth year of labour, and not with the ecclesiastical year, on the first of Abib (Nisan), and that it lasted till the autumn of the seventh year, when the cultivation of the land would commence again with the preparation of the ground and the sowing of the seed for the eighth year; and with this the command to proclaim the jubilee year on “the tenth day of the seventh month” throughout all the land (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.9">Lev 25:9</reference>), and the calculation in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.21">Lev 25:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.22">Lev 25:22</reference>, fully agree.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.25.5">Lev 25:5</reference> <div eID="gen1498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1499" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">That which has fallen out </hi>(been shaken out) <hi type="italic">of thy harvest</hi> (i.e., the corn which had grown from the grains of the previous harvest that had fallen out) <hi type="italic">thou shalt not reap, and the grapes of thine uncut thou shalt not gather</hi>.” נזיר, the Nazarite, who let his hair grow freely without cutting it (Num 6:5), is used figuratively, both here and in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.11">Lev 25:11</reference>, to denote a vine not pruned, since by being left to put forth all its productive power it was consecrated to the Lord. The Roman poets employ a similar figure, and speak of the <hi type="italic">viridis coma</hi> of the vine (<hi type="italic">Tibull</hi>. i. 7, 34; <hi type="italic">Propert</hi>. ii. 15, 12).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.25.6-Lev.25.7">Lev 25:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen1499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1500" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And the Sabbath of the land</hi> (i.e., the produce of the sabbatical year or year of rest, whatever grew that year without cultivation) <hi type="italic">shall be to you for food, for thee and thy servant,...and for the beasts that are in thy land shall all its produce be for food</hi>.” The meaning is, that what grew of itself was not to be reaped by the owner of the land, but that masters and servants, labourers and visitors, cattle and game, were to eat thereof away from the field (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.25.12">Lev 25:12</reference>). The produce arising without tilling or sowing was to be a common good for man and beast. According to <reference osisRef="Exod.23.11">Exo 23:11</reference>, it was to belong to the poor and needy; but the owner was not forbidden to partake of it also, so that there can be no discrepancy discovered between this passage and the verse before us. The produce referred to would be by no means inconsiderable, particularly if there had not been a careful gleaning after the harvest, or the corn had become over-ripe. In the fertile portions of Palestine, especially in the plain of Jezreel and on the table-land of Galilee, as well as in other parts, large quantities of wheat and other cereals are still self-sown from the ripe ears, the over-flowing of which is not gathered by any of the inhabitants of the land. <hi type="italic">Strabo</hi> gives a similar account of Albania, viz., that in many parts a field once sown will bear fruit twice and even three times, the first yield being as much as fifty-fold. The intention of his law was not so much to secure the physical recreation of both the land and people, however useful and necessary this might be for men, animals, and land in this sublunary world; but the land was to keep Sabbath to the Lord in the seventh year. In the sabbatical year the land, which the Lord had given to His people, was to observe a period of holy rest and refreshment to its Lord and God, just as the congregation did on the Sabbath-day; and the hand of man was to be withheld from the fields and fruit-gardens from working them, that they might yield their produce for his use. The earth was to be saved from the hand of man exhausting its power for earthly purposes as his own property, and to enjoy the holy rest with which God had blessed the earth and all its productions after the creation. From this, Israel, as the nation of God, was to learn, on the one hand, that although the earth was created for man, it was not merely created for him to draw out its powers for his own use, but also to be holy to the Lord, and participate in His blessed rest; and on the other hand, that the great purpose for which the congregation of the Lord existed, did not consist in the uninterrupted tilling of the earth, connected with bitter labour in the sweat of his brow (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.17">Gen 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.19">Gen 3:19</reference>), but in the peaceful enjoyment of the fruits of the earth, which the Lord their God had given them, and would give them still without the labour of their hands, if they strove to keep His covenant and satisfy themselves with His grace. This intention of the sabbatical year comes out still more plainly in the year of jubilee, in which the idea of the sanctification of the whole land as the Lord’s property is still more strongly expressed, and whose inward connection with the sabbatical year is indicated by the fact that the time for observing it was regulated by the sabbatical years (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.8">Lev 25:8</reference>). <div eID="gen1500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1501" type="x-p"/> The law for the Year of Jubilee refers first of all to its observance (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.8-Lev.25.12">Lev 25:8-12</reference>), and secondly to its effects (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) upon the possession of property (vv. 13-34), and (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) upon the personal freedom of the Israelites (vv. 35-55).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.25.8-Lev.25.9">Lev 25:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen1501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1502" type="x-p"/> Keeping the year of jubilee. <reference osisRef="Lev.25.8">Lev 25:8</reference>, Lev 25:9. Seven Sabbaths of years - i.e., year-Sabbaths or sabbatical years, or seven times seven years, the time of seven year-Sabbaths, that is to say, 49 years - they were to count, and then at the expiration of that time to cause the trumpet of jubilee to go (sound) through the whole land on the tenth of the seventh month, i.e., the day of atonement, to proclaim the entrance of the year of jubilee. This mode of announcement was closely connected with the idea of the year itself. The blowing of trumpets, or blast of the far-sounding horn (<hi type="italic">shophar</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Lev.23.24">Lev 23:24</reference>), was the signal of the descent of the Lord upon Sinai, to raise Israel to be His people, to receive them into His covenant, to unite them to Himself, and bless them through His covenant of grace (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.13">Exo 19:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">Exo 19:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.19">Exo 19:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.20.18">Exo 20:18</reference>). Just as the people were to come up to the mountain at the sounding of the יובל, or the voice of the <hi type="italic">shophar</hi>, to commemorate its union with the Lord, so at the expiration of the seventh sabbatical year the trumpet-blast was to announce to the covenant nation the gracious presence of its God, and the coming of the year which was to bring “liberty throughout the land to all that dwelt therein” (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.10">Lev 25:10</reference>), - deliverance from bondage (Lev 25:40.), return to their property and family (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.10">Lev 25:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.13">Lev 25:13</reference>), and release from the bitter labour of cultivating the land (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.11">Lev 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.12">Lev 25:12</reference>). This year of grace as proclaimed and began with the day of atonement of every seventh sabbatical year, to show that it was only with the full forgiveness of sins that the blessed liberty of the children of God could possibly commence. This grand year of grace was to return after seven times seven years; i.e., as is expressly stated in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.10">Lev 25:10</reference>, every fiftieth year was to be sanctified as a year of jubilee. By this regulation of the time, the view held by <hi type="italic">R. Jehuda,</hi> and the chronologists and antiquarians who have followed him, that every seventh sabbatical year, i.e., the 49th year, was to be kept as the year of jubilee, is proved to be at variance with the text, and the fiftieth year is shown to be the year of rest, in which the sabbatical idea attained its fullest realization, and reached its earthly temporal close.
entries.content_plain:
Lev 25:8-9 
 
 Keeping the year of jubilee. Lev 25:8, Lev 25:9. Seven Sabbaths of years - i.e., year-Sabbaths or sabbatical years, or seven times seven years, the time of seven year-Sabbaths, that is to say, 49 years - they were to count, and then at the expiration of that time to cause the trumpet of jubilee to go (sound) through the whole land on the tenth of the seventh month, i.e., the day of atonement, to proclaim the entrance of the year of jubilee. The blowing of trumpets, or blast of the far-sounding horn (shophar, see at Lev 23:24), was the signal of the descent of the Lord upon Sinai, to raise Israel to be His people, to receive them into His covenant, to unite them to Himself, and bless them through His covenant of grace (Exo 19:13, Exo 19:16, Exo 19:19; Exo 20:18). entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.25.10">Lev 25:10</reference> <div eID="gen1502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1503" type="x-p"/> The words, “Ye shall proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof,” are more closely defined by the two clauses commencing with היא יובל in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.10">Lev 25:10</reference> and Lev 25:11. “A trumpet-blast shall it be to you, that ye return every one to his own possession, and every one to his family:” a still further explanation is given in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.23-Lev.25.34">Lev 25:23-34</reference> and 39-55. This was to be the fruit or effect of the blast, i.e., of the year commencing with the blast, and hence the year was called “the year of liberty,” or free year, in Eze 46:17. יובל, from יבל to flow with a rushing noise, does not mean jubilation or the time of jubilation (<hi type="italic">Ges.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Kn</hi>., and others); but wherever it is not applied to the year of jubilee, it signifies only the loud blast of a trumpet (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.13">Exo 19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.6.5">Jos 6:5</reference>). This meaning also applies here in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Lev.25.10">Lev 25:10</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.11">Lev 25:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.25.12">Lev 25:12</reference>; whilst in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.15">Lev 25:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.28">Lev 25:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.30">Lev 25:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.31">Lev 25:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.33">Lev 25:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.18">Lev 27:18</reference>, and Num 36:4, it is used as an abbreviated expression for יובל שׁנת, the year of the trumpet-blast.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.25.11-Lev.25.12">Lev 25:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen1503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1504" type="x-p"/> The other effect of the fiftieth year proclaimed with the trumpet-blast consisted in the fact that the Israelites were not to sow or reap, just as in the sabbatical year (see <reference osisRef="Lev.25.4">Lev 25:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.5">Lev 25:5</reference>). “For it is יובל,” i.e., not “jubilation or time of jubilation,” but “the time or year of the trumpet-blast, it shall be holy to you,” i.e., a sabbatical time, which is to be holy to you like the day of the trumpet-blast (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.23">Lev 25:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.24">Lev 25:24</reference>).

entries.content_osis: Leviticus 25:35-55 <div eID="gen1515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1516" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">second</hi> effect of the jubilee year, viz., <hi type="italic">the return of an Israelite, who had become a slave, to liberty and to his family,</hi> is also introduced with an exhortation to support an impoverished brother (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.35-Lev.25.38">Lev 25:35-38</reference>), and preserve to him his personal freedom.  <reference osisRef="Lev.25.35">Lev 25:35</reference> “If thy brother (countryman, or member of the same tribe) becomes poor, and his hand trembles by thee, thou shalt lay hold of him;” i.e., if he is no longer able to sustain himself alone, thou shalt take him by the arm to help him out of his misfortune. “Let him live with thee as a stranger and sojourner.” וחי introduces the apodosis (see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §126, note 1).
